objectives: Explain what the price elasticity of demand means, and tell elastic demand from inelastic demand.
Calculate price elasticity with the midpoint method, and explain how elasticity relates to total revenue.
Analyze how a supply shock affects prices, producer revenue, and food security when food demand is inelastic.

concepts.definition: The percentage change in quantity demanded when the price changes by 1%. It is usually stated as an absolute value.
If the elasticity (absolute value) is greater than 1, demand is elastic; if it is less than 1, demand is inelastic; if it equals 1, demand is unit elastic.
A way to calculate percentage changes by dividing by the average of the starting and ending values instead of the starting value. It gives the same result whether the price rises or falls.
Total revenue = price × quantity sold. When demand is inelastic, raising the price increases total revenue; when demand is elastic, it decreases total revenue.
Food is a necessity that is hard to replace, so demand for it is usually inelastic. As a result, even a small change in supply can move the price a lot.

beginner.summary: For things people really need, like rice, the amount people buy barely drops when the price goes up. For things people can do without, like chips, it drops a lot. How sensitive buyers are to price is called elasticity.

sections.heading: How strongly do buyers react?
paragraphs: If the price of chips goes up, you can just buy a different snack or skip it, so the amount people buy drops a lot. We call goods like this elastic.
For essentials like rice or medicine, it is hard to cut back much even when the price rises. We call goods like this inelastic.

sections.heading: Comparing percentage changes
paragraphs: To find elasticity, divide the percentage change in the amount people buy by the percentage change in the price. Because it looks at percentages, not the number of items, you can compare expensive goods with cheap ones. For an exact answer, you calculate each percentage using the value halfway between the before and after amounts. This is called the midpoint method.

sections.heading: Does raising the price bring a store more money?
paragraphs: A store's revenue is price × number of items sold. If customers barely cut back when the price goes up (inelastic), revenue rises. If many customers stop buying (elastic), revenue actually falls.

sections.heading: Why do food prices swing so much?
paragraphs: People cannot easily eat much less when food prices rise. So after a poor harvest, even a small drop in the rice supply can push the price up a lot. After a bumper crop, the opposite happens: the price can fall so far that farmers end up earning less.

intermediate.summary: Price elasticity of demand = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price, calculated with the midpoint method. Elasticity is a key tool for explaining changes in total revenue and the effects of supply shocks.

sections.heading: Definition and categories
paragraphs: Price elasticity of demand = |percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price|. If the value is greater than 1, demand is elastic; if less than 1, inelastic; if exactly 1, unit elastic.

What determines elasticity: whether close substitutes exist, whether the good is a necessity or a luxury, whether it takes up a large share of income, and whether buyers have enough time to respond (demand is more elastic over longer periods).

sections.heading: The midpoint method
paragraphs: Percentage change = (ending value − starting value) ÷ ((starting value + ending value) ÷ 2). Calculate this for both quantity and price, then divide. Because it uses the average as the base, it gives the same elasticity whether the price rises or falls.

sections.heading: The total revenue rule
paragraphs: Inelastic demand: price↑ → total revenue↑, price↓ → total revenue↓. Elastic demand: price↑ → total revenue↓, price↓ → total revenue↑. With unit elastic demand, total revenue stays about the same when the price changes.

sections.heading: Food markets and inelastic demand
paragraphs: Demand for food is usually inelastic, so the demand curve is steep. On a steep demand curve, the same shift in supply produces a large change in price and a small change in quantity.

That is why a poor harvest tends to cause price spikes and hardship for consumers, while a bumper harvest tends to cause price crashes and lower farm income. Movements in world food prices are tracked continuously by indicators such as the FAO Food Price Index.

advanced.summary: Elasticity is ε = (ΔQ/Q̄)/(ΔP/P̄), and along a linear demand curve its value differs from point to point. How total revenue responds to price, how supply shocks affect prices, and how a tax burden is shared (tax incidence) can all be explained by relative elasticities.

sections.heading: Definition and point elasticity
paragraphs: Point elasticity is ε = (dQ/dP)·(P/Q). For linear demand Q = a − bP, ε = −bP/(a − bP), so even with a constant slope, |ε| is larger at higher prices (smaller quantities). To be precise, a statement like "demand for this good is elastic" should say which price range it refers to.

sections.heading: Arc elasticity: the midpoint formula
paragraphs: The arc elasticity between two points (P₁, Q₁) and (P₂, Q₂) is ε = [(Q₂ − Q₁)/((Q₁ + Q₂)/2)] ÷ [(P₂ − P₁)/((P₁ + P₂)/2)]. This removes the problem of the result depending on which point you start from.

sections.heading: How total revenue responds to price
paragraphs: With TR = P·Q(P), dTR/dP = Q·(1 + ε), where ε is negative. If |ε| < 1, dTR/dP > 0, so a price increase raises total revenue; if |ε| > 1, the opposite holds. Total revenue is at its maximum at the point where |ε| = 1.

sections.heading: Supply shocks and tax incidence
paragraphs: When supply falls by ΔS, the change in the equilibrium price is roughly inversely related to the slopes (elasticities) of demand and supply. The less elastic demand is, the larger the price change from the same supply shock. This is why prices are so volatile in markets with inelastic demand, such as food.

By the same logic, when a good is taxed, the less elastic side (the side that finds it harder to respond) bears more of the tax. A tax on food can fall largely on consumers, especially low-income households that spend a large share of their income on food.

worked_examples.title: A simple elasticity calculation
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: The price of rice rose by 10%, and the quantity of rice demanded fell by 2%. What is the elasticity, and is demand elastic or inelastic?
steps: Elasticity = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price = 2% ÷ 10%.
It is less than 1, so demand is inelastic.

worked_examples.title: The midpoint method
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: When the price of a pack of instant noodles rose from $1.00 to $1.20, daily sales at a convenience store fell from 500 packs to 450 packs. Use the midpoint method to find the elasticity.

worked_examples.title: The price that maximizes total revenue
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: Daily demand for tickets to a show is Q = 120 − 4P, where P is in dollars and Q is the number of people. What price maximizes total revenue, and what is total revenue at that price?
steps: Total revenue TR = P × Q = P(120 − 4P) = 120P − 4P².
Differentiate TR with respect to P and set it to 0: 120 − 8P = 0 → P = 15.

Check: point elasticity ε = (dQ/dP)·(P/Q) = −4 × 15/60 = −1. This matches the rule that total revenue is largest where |ε| = 1. At P = 14, TR = 14 × 64 = 896, and at P = 16, TR = 16 × 56 = 896; both are less than 900.
worked_examples.answer: Total revenue is largest, at $900, when the price is $15.

worked_examples.title: Who pays the tax? (tax incidence)
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: In a market with Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 10 + P (equilibrium price before the tax: P = 30), sellers must pay a tax of 3 per unit. What price do consumers pay, what price do sellers receive, and how is the tax of 3 split between them?
steps: Let Pp be the price sellers receive. Supply is Qs = 10 + Pp, and the consumer price is Pc = Pp + 3.

At the pre-tax equilibrium, the elasticity of demand is |−2 × 30/40| = 1.5 and the elasticity of supply is 1 × 30/40 = 0.75, so supply is less elastic. The less elastic side (sellers) bears more of the tax.
worked_examples.answer: Consumers pay 31 and sellers receive 28. Consumers bear 1 of the tax and sellers bear 2.

graphs.title: A decrease in supply with inelastic demand
graphs.caption: Hypothetical example. With a steep (inelastic) demand curve, when supply falls from S1 to S2, the price rises sharply from 40 to 50 (up 25%), while quantity falls only slightly from 40 to 35 (down 12.5%).

real_world_examples.title: Why a bumper crop can lower farm income
paragraphs: When food demand is inelastic, a bumper crop that sharply increases output can make the price fall by a larger percentage than output rises. Farm total revenue, which is price × quantity sold, then actually falls. This is one reason farm prices swing so much from year to year.

real_world_examples.title: Indicators that track world food prices
paragraphs: The FAO Food Price Index is published monthly. It tracks changes in world prices of cereals, vegetable oils, dairy, meat, and sugar, weighted by each group's share of exports. The World Bank regularly reviews food price inflation in countries around the world to report on food security. As a class activity, you can look up the latest figures yourself and interpret them using the idea of elasticity.

sdg_case.title: Inelastic food demand, price volatility, and food waste
paragraphs: SDG target 2.c calls for well-functioning food markets and timely access to market information, including information on food reserves, to help limit extreme food price volatility. SDG target 12.3 calls for halving per capita food waste at the retail and consumer levels and reducing food losses along production and supply chains.

If food demand is inelastic, even a small wobble in supply can move prices a lot. From this point of view, compare which policies could reduce price swings and the burden on vulnerable households, and what assumptions each policy depends on.

options.name: Public market information and food reserve systems
benefits: Transparent information on production and stocks can reduce panic buying and overreactions in prices.
Reserves act as a buffer during supply shocks.
costs: Maintaining reserves and information systems costs money.
assumptions: The information is reliable, and market participants respond to it.

options.name: Cut or remove taxes on food
costs: Tax revenue falls, and better-off households benefit too.
If demand is inelastic, lower prices do not raise consumption much.
assumptions: The tax cut is actually passed on to consumer prices.

options.name: Reduce food loss and food waste
benefits: Food that would have been thrown away stays on the market, so the same production can feed more people (similar to an increase in supply).
Reduces wasted resources and environmental pressure (SDG 12).
costs: Investing in storage and distribution and changing consumer habits take time and money.
assumptions: Lower losses actually translate into more food supplied to the market.

discussion: Because food demand is inelastic, some policies become more effective and others less effective. Re-evaluate each option from this point of view.

key_takeaways: Elasticity measures how sensitive quantity demanded is to price changes; using 1 as the dividing line, demand is classified as elastic or inelastic.
The midpoint method gives the same elasticity regardless of the direction of the change.
When demand is inelastic, a price increase raises total revenue, and supply shocks lead to large price swings. Food markets are a classic example.
